idiom_name: protocol reply-to header plus an ephemeral reply channel owned by the requester
implementation_notes: No language makes the return address automatic: the request must carry the destination of its reply as transport metadata and the replier must route to it. On a broker that is the protocol's reply-to property (AMQP reply-to, JMS JMSReplyTo, MQTT 5 Response Topic, NATS reply subject) plus a reply channel the requester owns; inside a process it is a reply handle placed in the request value (channel, promise, continuation). Either way the address must be validated before it is used for routing, paired with a correlation identifier, and given a lifetime.
code_sketch:
request.metadata["reply-to"]      = "orders.reply.client-42"   # temp queue / inbox / topic
request.metadata["correlation-id"]  = "7f3c9e"
request.metadata["expiration"]      = 30000
send("orders.queue", request)

# replier: the address is data, so validate it before publishing
send(request.metadata["reply-to"], reply,
     correlation_id=request.metadata["correlation-id"])
pitfalls: An address that is used without validation turns the replier into an open relay: any producer can steer its answers to an arbitrary destination.
Treating the address as 'just a header' hides its lifecycle — the channel behind it must still exist when the reply arrives, or the answer is lost silently.
A return address without a correlation identifier only works while the reply channel is unique per request; shared channels need both.
sources: Hohpe, G. and Woolf, B. (2003). Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions. Addison-Wesley — 'Message Construction': Return Address.
